title: U.S. House · Texas's 31st Congressional District
area: Central Texas, primarily Williamson County (Round Rock, Georgetown) and part of Bell County (Killeen).

context.text: Texas redrew its congressional district boundaries in August 2025 ahead of the 2026 elections, a mid-decade redistricting.

In the March 3, 2026 primaries, incumbent John Carter won the Republican nomination with 59.7% of the vote in a ten-candidate field, and Justin Early defeated Stuart Whitlow 57.6% to 42.4% for the Democratic nomination. Greg Stoker advanced as the Green Party's nominee from its March 21, 2026 convention.

summary.text: John Carter is the incumbent Republican U.S. Representative for Texas's 31st District, a former Williamson County district court judge who chairs the House Appropriations Military Construction-Veterans Affairs subcommittee.

background.text: Born in Houston, Texas; earned a B.A. from Texas Tech University in 1964 and a J.D. from the University of Texas in 1969.
Served as a District Court Judge in Williamson County, Texas, from 1981 to 2001; first elected to Congress in 2002.

positions.summary: Says he supported the American Health Care Act of 2017, which he describes as repealing and replacing the Affordable Care Act.
positions.quote: I supported the American Health Care Act of 2017. This act would repeal Obamacare and replace it with a far more equitable solution that would benefit small businesses and Americans struggling with health care costs.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Appropriations and chairs its Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies subcommittee in the 119th Congress.

candidates.name: Justin Early
candidates.ballotNote: Won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary with 57.6% of the vote

summary.text: Justin Early is a U.S. Army veteran and cybersecurity professional who won the Democratic primary to challenge Rep. John Carter.

background.text: Graduated from Leander High School in 1998; served in the U.S. Army as a paratrooper and later worked as a LAN systems administrator at the Defense Intelligence Agency; his career includes work in cybersecurity.
Has served as a Democratic precinct chair in Tarrant County and as a presidential delegate in 2008.

priorities.text: His campaign website lists veterans' healthcare funding, clearing VA claims backlogs, and workplace protections such as paid family and sick leave among his priorities.
In a Community Impact candidate Q&A, lists lowering costs for working families, responsible AI and data protection, and strengthening democracy as his top priorities.
priorities.quote: Lowering costs for working families, responsible AI and data protection, and strengthening democracy.

positions.summary: Says he would work to shift the tax burden off working families, saying people should not pay a higher share than the wealthiest.
positions.quote: Lower taxes for everyday Americans—if you work hard, you shouldn't pay more than billionaires. Let's shift the tax burden off working families and onto those who can afford it.

positions.summary: Says he will resist a national school voucher scheme and keep public dollars in public schools.
positions.quote: Resist any attempts to impose a national school voucher scheme. Public dollars belong in public schools, not diverted to unaccountable private or religious institutions.

statements.quote: Overturn Trump-era policies that weaponized immigration enforcement against communities of color. I will ensure that immigration enforcement focuses on real threats, not sowing fear in immigrant neighborhoods.
statements.context: On the immigration section of his campaign issues page

statements.quote: Support America's first responders—police, fire, and EMS—so they can do their jobs effectively. First responders put their lives on the line for us. I'll make sure they have the resources and support they need to stay safe and save lives.
statements.context: On the security section of his campaign issues page

candidates.name: Greg Stoker
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced as the Green Party's nominee from its March 21, 2026 state convention

summary.text: Greg Stoker is the Green Party nominee in this race; little public biographical or policy information is available.

priorities.text: In his January 2026 campaign launch video, said his new type of politics starts with affordability and accountability for officials.
priorities.quote: It starts with affordability for us, and accountability for officials who sell out Texas to corporations and foreign interests

priorities.text: Said he will not accept money from political action committees or corporate donors, per Middle East Eye.

researchNotes: Carter's positions are limited to official committee assignments; no 2026 Candidate Connection survey was found for him. Justin Early's positions and statements come from his campaign issues page (read in a headless browser) and a Community Impact Q&A; no statements on abortion, guns, the minimum wage or other guide issues were found on his site. No biography, campaign website, or Candidate Connection survey was found for Greg Stoker on Ballotpedia; his campaign site (stokerfortexas.com) is behind a bot-verification page and was not read. His entry draws only on press coverage of his January 2026 announcement and is minimal. Federal key votes and FEC totals for the incumbent are added separately by script.
